classroom.beats.0.text: Ten {people} get the same case question.
classroom.beats.1.text: Each asks the school's AI for an outline. They come back alike.
classroom.page.setup: Ten {people} in a strategy {group} each use the school's AI to help answer the same case question: how should an industrial-equipment maker respond to a low-cost competitor? The {group} allows AI, and each {person} says they used it. Each writes their own plan, and each plan holds up when read alone. What can still go wrong is institutional monoculture: shared systems and defaults narrow the range of frames a group considers. The case is an illustration based on Romasanta, Thomas & Levina (2026), a study of AI models' strategy advice, and Bottesch (2025), a field experiment with knowledge workers at an industrial company. Neither study looked at students. The {group}, the case and the plans are constructed.
classroom.page.srSummary: An animated figure that opens on its name, Institutional monoculture, failure mode 6 of 7. Ten red dots stand for ten {people} in a strategy {group} with an example task, a case question: how should we respond to a low-cost competitor? The context lists its prices, our patents, dealers, price-led buyers and service revenue. Each {person} asks the school's AI for an outline, and ten grey outlines come back in the same pattern. Each {person} writes their own plan, in ten different layouts, all marked "All drafted with AI". {reviewer_sees} that each plan holds up, and the ticks stay. {reviewer_lines} up the one-line problem statement from every finished plan: "How do we stand out?", "Why pay more for ours?", "Why are we worth more?", "What can't they copy?", "Where do we add value?", "Can we stay premium?", "Can we out-serve them?", "Which features win?", "Can we keep our edge?", "What earns a premium?". Each line is read, and a bracket closes around all ten, labelled "One frame: differentiate". {reviewer_sees} only the finished plans, but the figure shows the viewer where the frame came from: a grey card comes out of the AI box, saying almost every outline opened with "Differentiate on value", labelled "Not seen by {reviewer}". A dashed grey line runs from it to the bracket, which turns grey, with a grey tag: "AI's frame". {reviewer_ask} what frames are missing: a dashed box with that question appears beside the bracket. Next, while the first run dims above, the figure imagines {reviewer} sending the plans back: a navy line runs from the question box to the heading "Sent back: what else could the problem be?", over the same {group}, imagined. Each {person} writes the problem in red first, then asks the AI to challenge it ("What did you assume? What other frames fit?"), and a grey speech bubble appears on each plan before they write. These plans hold up too. Their problems are lined up under the heading in three groups, with a line under them: more frames to weigh before the {group} chooses. The groups: differentiate ("How do we stand out?", "Why pay more for ours?", "Why are we worth more?"); match on cost ("Can we win on cost?", "Who buys on price?", "Can we cut unit costs?", "Who is switching?"); partner or license ("Should we partner?", "Who wants our designs?", "Is the rival a buyer?"). The figure ends on the {check_l}, with the source under the picture. Each beat is listed below with what is on screen.
classroom.page.study.3: Neither study looked at students, lined up a {group}'s plans or tested defining the problem first. Bottesch's participants were knowledge workers at one industrial company. The lineup and the imagined {group} are this figure's illustration of what the findings could mean for a {group} that drafts with one AI.
classroom.page.linksNote: The failure mode and the {check_l} come from the original essay. This page shows the same move in a strategy {group} working a company's case.

page.title: Institutional monoculture
page.description: Ten plans drafted with the same AI can each pass review and still share one definition of the problem. Lining up their problem statements shows it.
page.setup: Ten {people} at an industrial-equipment maker each use the company's AI to help answer the CEO's question: how should we respond to a low-cost competitor? Each writes their own plan, and each plan holds up when read alone. What can still go wrong is institutional monoculture: shared systems and defaults narrow the range of frames a group considers. It can happen wherever people ask the same AI, like a nonprofit's program team asking how to respond to a funder's new priority. Illustration based on Romasanta, Thomas & Levina (2026) and Bottesch (2025). The {group}, the question and the plans are constructed.

checkLines: What frames are missing across the {group}?
Line up the problems. What else could the problem be?
page.checkFollow: Read one at a time, every plan holds up. The plans differ in their details, like names, numbers and products, but lined up, they share one problem definition, the one almost every AI outline opened with. {Reviewer} never sees those outlines; the lineup of finished plans is enough to show the shared frame. Lining up shows which frames a {group} has. It can't show which are missing. For that, {reviewer_ask_l} what else the problem could be, drawing on their own knowledge of the market or on frames the {group} names before discussion settles on one. In the imagined rerun {reviewer_sends} the plans back with that question. {Each_person} then writes a problem frame without AI and asks an AI to find assumptions they missed and suggest other frames, as the original essay, *The Irreducible Officer*, proposes. Whether framing first spreads frames across a {group} is untested, and the imagined rerun is one possible answer. Agreement can also come from a shared purpose or strong evidence, and a different frame isn't better by itself. A {group} can compare several frames and still agree on one.

about.text: Each plan's first line is its problem statement: the question the plan sets out to answer. The figure groups problems by the goal they set, and names three goals for the imagined {group} as one possible answer. Telling real frames apart takes reading. The plans, their problem lines and the AI's opening line are constructed. They don't show the output of any model or the plans of any real company.

study: Romasanta, Thomas and Levina asked leading AI models for strategic advice. Their summary of the work reports: "Across thousands of simulations, we saw LLMs almost uniformly select the same trendy strategies, regardless of context." They name the pattern: "We call the propensity for AI to opt for buzzy ideas over reasoned solutions 'trendslop.'"

That summary names no strategies, and the *Harvard Business Review* article itself, a practitioner piece, is paywalled. Coverage of the article reports that the models' defaults included differentiation over commoditization, along with augmentation over automation and the long term over the short term. The figure's AI frame, "Differentiate on value", follows that reported default. The plans and their problem lines are constructed.

Bottesch ran a field experiment with "99 knowledge workers from a multinational industrial corporation" and found "that indeed significant homogenisation effects occur in terms of style and content when knowledge workers are supported by GenAI (versus when they are not)". The abstract also offers "initial evidence that these effects might be mitigated through advanced prompting and (more) critical handling of GenAI output by knowledge workers." It is a single-author conference paper from one company, and the abstract gives no effect sizes. The figure draws the plans in different layouts so the shared frame has something to hide behind; Bottesch found that style converged as well.

Neither study lined up a team's plans or tested defining the problem first. The lineup and the imagined {group} are this figure's illustration of what the findings could mean for a team that drafts with one AI.

Counter-evidence: Terwiesch et al. (*Production and Operations Management*, 2026) found that better prompting, assigned personas and pooling several vendors brought the diversity of AI-generated ideas close to human levels. With Bottesch's mitigation finding, that suggests sameness is the default, and deliberate design can push against it.

Sources: Romasanta, Thomas & Levina, "Researchers Asked LLMs for Strategic Advice. They Got 'Trendslop' in Return," *Harvard Business Review* (March 2026), quoted from the authors' summary on NYU Stern's research highlights page; the reported defaults are from coverage of the article. Bottesch, "Towards Generative Monoculture? Insights from a Field Experiment on Style and Content Homogenisation Effects in GenAI-Supported Knowledge Work," ACIS 2025 Proceedings, quoted from the abstract. The {group}, the question, the plans and the AI's outlines are constructed. The figure shows none of either study's data.
